response.title: Will a power station run my RV furnace fan all night when it's near freezing, so my trailer battery isn't dead by morning?
response.answer:
Yes—a portable power station can run your RV furnace fan all night, even when it's near freezing. But you'll need the right battery capacity and a safe way to connect it to your furnace.

Most RV propane furnaces use propane for heat and 12V DC electricity to power the blower fan, ignition, and control board. The fan can draw enough power to drain a typical trailer battery overnight.

How big a power station do you need?

For a typical RV propane furnace, assuming 8 hours of overnight heating:

Power station capacity

	

Estimated furnace runtime




300Wh

	

4–7 hours




500Wh

	

7–12 hours




1,000Wh

	

14–24 hours




2,000Wh

	

28–48 hours

These are rough estimates assuming a furnace drawing 80–120 watts while running, cycling on and off about 50–70% of the night, and accounting for some conversion losses.

MY SIZING RECOMMENDATION

1,000Wh

Good starting point for an 8–10-hour cold night

If the furnace runs nearly continuously because it's very cold or the trailer has poor insulation, you'll need substantially more capacity.

How to connect it

The important detail is that your RV furnace usually doesn't have a plug you can connect directly to a power station.

There are two main approaches:

Power the RV's 12V system: Use a properly rated, fused DC connection or a compatible battery-charging setup. Many power stations have 12V cigarette-lighter outputs limited to 10A, which may be insufficient for the furnace's startup current and other RV loads.

Use the power station's 120V AC outlet: If your RV has a compatible shore-power connection, you can use an appropriately rated adapter to supply the RV converter, which then powers the 12V system. This is simpler in some setups, but inverter and converter losses reduce runtime. Verify that the RV converter doesn't overload the station or waste power charging the trailer battery.

Keep the power station inside its rated operating-temperature range. Lithium batteries generally cannot be charged below freezing unless they have suitable low-temperature protection. Also, don't bypass the RV's battery protection, furnace safety controls, or CO/propane detectors.

Let me calculate what you'll actually need

I have three questions:

What RV or travel trailer do you have? (Brand, model, and year if known.)

What battery is currently installed? For example, one 12V lead-acid battery, two 6V batteries, or a lithium battery.

What power station do you have or plan to buy? For example, EcoFlow, Jackery, Bluetti, or Anker.

With those details, I can estimate whether a 500Wh or 1,000Wh station will keep your furnace running until morning and recommend the safest way to avoid draining your trailer battery.
